Build the gamification around one central currency (like XP, Karma or fin bits) that is earned by the core actions and shows progress.
Show people both what they have accomplished and how much is left, such as the share of a course or goal completed.
Tie rewards to the user's real goals so they mean something; do not hand out meaningless rewards.
Animate a hover pop-up like the name tag from slightly lower at opacity zero, using Smart Animate with a custom spring rather than the default easing.
Explain icon-only controls with a tooltip that appears only after the pointer rests on the icon for a full second, and return to the original state on mouse leave.
In a swipeable card stack, while the top card is dragged away, move the cards behind down and scale them up to fill its place.
In lists and line items, align text hard left and values such as prices hard right; centre only content people are not meant to read.
Don't fill empty space in a card by adding more content; look for the edges where content can be placed instead.

In compact components (cards, chat inputs, Kanban cards, sidebars, checklists), place every element against at least two edges, counting card sides and edges created by other elements such as an avatar and name.
values: at least two or more edges

results.rule: Don't fix a crowded card by hiding secondary actions in a corner menu; move content to clear up edges, or manufacture a new edge that lines buttons and avatar up into a solid line for the content below.
Don't rely on extra white space alone to fix a dense list; differentiate the content instead.
Differentiate dense lists: show avatars wherever people are referenced and group items by a meaningful key such as due date.
When something is unclear, turn plain text into immediately recognisable icons, diagrams or chips instead of adding comparisons, labels or tooltips.
Don't depend on icon-only actions whose meaning only becomes clear once a tooltip appears; use visuals people recognise immediately, or placement that explains the control.
Keep a checkbox's off state plain (thin border, no color, no icon) and give fill, color and a checkmark only to the on state.
Show values that are on their default state in gray so non-default values catch the eye.
To make one element stand out, change its surroundings instead of giving it more color or bolder text.
Don't structure an open canvas by stacking containers and cards; use a single line and a column edge, with sections for grouping.
Use sections (or tabs) to group content so people never scan one long undifferentiated list.
Judge a screen by how fast someone can find one thing, since people arrive with a question and hunt for the answer.
Collect inspiration from competitors and sibling products, and search for existing assets, before you start designing.
On an AI product landing page, use a search or prompt bar the visitor can type into as the hero call to action instead of a plain button.
Merge landing pages that sell the same thing into one page built around the few key points they share.
Make a section work through layout alone; it should already look good before any animation is added.
Include a privacy section on the landing page of any software or hardware that handles user data.
Try several layouts for a key section like the final CTA, and keep changing it until it feels right.
Install the sonner package from the command line; this page's command is pnpm i sonner.
Add the <Toaster /> component to the app before calling toast(); the example mounts it inside <body>, after {children}, in the root layout.tsx.
Import Toaster and toast as named imports from the 'sonner' package.
Show a toast by calling toast() with the message string from an event handler, for example a button's onClick.
Use Sonner as the toast component in React projects. [inferred]
Install Sonner with npm install sonner.
Render the <Toaster /> component in the root of the app.
Show a toast by calling toast() with the message, and pass extra options as an object in the second argument.
To change a toast that is already on screen, call toast() with its id and pass only the properties you want to change, instead of showing a new toast. [inferred]
values: toast('Toast has been updated', { id: toastId, })

results.rule: Keep the id that toast() returns whenever you may need to update or dismiss that toast later.
Change a toast's type on update by calling the typed function, such as toast.success() or toast.error(), with the same id.
values: toast.success('Toast has been updated', { id: toastId, })

results.rule: Use onDismiss for user dismissal (the close button or a swipe) and onAutoClose for the toast timing out; do not treat them as the same event.
Remove a toast from code with toast.dismiss(id).
In Astro projects that use view transitions, or that hit any other Sonner issue, import Sonner's stylesheet in a layout file.

When rendering Sonner inside shadow DOM, add Sonner's styles to the shadow root manually; one documented way is to copy the <style> elements in document.head whose text includes '[data-sonner-toaster]' into the shadow root.
Style toasts beyond the default theme with the headless approach: no default styles and full control of the JSX (this is also the route for Tailwind).
Either keep Sonner's default look or go fully custom with headless; do not settle in between unless the change is small. [inferred]
For small changes such as the background color, set style in the Toaster's toastOptions so every toast gets the same styling.
Prefer the headless approach when styling toasts with classes.

When you only need to change a few things with classes, target the toast's elements through toastOptions.classNames (toast, title, description, actionButton, cancelButton, closeButton) and mark those styles !important.
When using Tailwind classes in classNames, mark each one important with the ! prefix.
Do not pile up many classNames or unstyled overrides; move to headless once the changes stop being small.
Call toast() with just a string when the toast only needs a title.
Set shared toast options on <Toaster />, and pass per-toast options as an object in toast()'s second argument; per-toast options win.
Use the success toast for success messages so a checkmark icon appears in front of the message.
Use the error toast for failures so an error icon appears in front of the message.
Use the action option to put a primary button in the toast; clicking it closes the toast and runs the callback passed via onClick.
Use the cancel option to put a secondary button in the toast; clicking it closes the toast and runs the callback passed via onClick.
Use a promise toast for async work, so the toast starts loading and switches to success or error on its own when the promise settles.
Pass functions as a promise toast's success and error messages so the message includes the promise's result or error.
Use a loading toast (spinner) only when you handle the loading, success and error states yourself; otherwise use a promise toast.
Set how long a toast stays on screen with the duration option; the default is 4000.
Give the toast container its accessible label through containerAriaLabel, which defaults to 'Notifications'.
Render the <Toaster /> component to display toasts; it can be placed anywhere in the app.
Visible toasts default to 3; change the count with the visibleToasts prop (the example uses 9).
Place toasts with the position prop, choosing top-left, top-center, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-center or bottom-right; the default is bottom-right.
Offsets default to 32px on desktop and 16px on mobile; change them with the offset and mobileOffset props.
Set mobile spacing with mobileOffset, which applies when the screen width is less than 600px.
Make the toaster follow the app's theme by wrapping it in a 'use client' component that passes the theme provider's resolvedTheme (for example from next-themes) to the theme prop.
Nail down a strong problem statement before anything else and open the case study with it; keep it clear and concise and back it with your research, as in the Emily Shen example.
Place a brief summary of the solution at the top, right after the problem, and expand on the process further down.
Keep case study text concise and include many images and GIFs that help explain it.
Give every chart a title, titles on the axes and a legend.
Build user personas from your data and centre them on the user's goals and frustrations as they relate to your problem and solution.
Don't spend time on persona details like finding a photo or picking a name, or on extraneous details unrelated to the problem.
Make low-fidelity wireframes (hand-drawn or in Figma) before high fidelity, and include preliminary or incomplete sketches in the case study.
Test lo-fi wireframes by having a couple of people go through them, observe whether things are intuitive, tweak, and test again before moving to the final design.
Present each final design with text next to it explaining the design choices and why it solves the problem.
Display design images as large as reasonably possible; don't squish many screens down.
End with a brief reflection covering what could be better, difficulties you hit, what you learned, and features or sections left out for time.
Keep the case study short enough to read in one sitting, favouring videos and images over text.
Make the case study skimmable with section titles that, like book chapter titles, summarize the content and make readers want to read more; avoid boring titles.
Test a page's structure by scrolling through it for 5 seconds: someone should be able to understand the idea in that time.
Don't cram a section with many components; use a clear grid-driven layout and give text and surrounding elements plenty of space.
Present content as blocks of text, simple illustrations and bold numbers instead of splitting text into separate elements with pop-ups, small ornamentation and complex shapes.
Don't tuck the product's name or what it does in a corner at a tiny size such as a 12 pixel font; make it prominent.
Show an image of the actual product, such as its dashboard, near the top of a software landing page.
Use scroll motion that deliberately draws attention to the product, for example morphing a hero image into the next section or fading the text out while the dashboard fades in.
Don't add complex animations just to have them; every animation should support clarity.
Don't use animations that only look cool while delaying the product until further down the page.
Once in a while, break the expected layout pattern with one unexpected, well-built moment, such as a hover effect or a page that unfolds on click.
In menus, use alignment and typography differences to show what is clickable, what isn't, and what is a keyboard shortcut.
Choose the direction of motion by meaning: slide temporary tools or actions up from the bottom, and slide screens from the left to show progress through an onboarding flow.
Judge the finished UI by whether every scroll, click and hover makes sense to the user.
Start a website by wireframing, and make the wireframe's layout varied rather than boring and average.
Do not repeat the same image-on-one-side, text-on-the-other column layout section after section; mix in a full-screen section, cards and a three-column section.
Use high-quality images.
Make an element bigger to draw attention to it and to add variety in sizes.
When making a dark mode, do not only change the background: flip the text to white and replace over-saturated primary and accent colors with lighter versions.
Replace plain white backgrounds with off-whites, or with a nondescript image background with a noise overlay for texture.
Weigh the reduced usability before adding motion sections like marquee text.
When a drawer does not touch the edge of the screen, adjust its animation with the --initial-transform CSS variable.
When you control the drawer with the open prop and need to react to Escape or outside clicks, also pass onOpenChange.
Keep the drawer's position corrected when the keyboard opens for an input inside it.
Turn on snapToSequentialPoint when every snap point in the drawer is equally important.
For product UI, do not rely on the 60-30-10 rule; plan color as four layers: neutral foundation, functional accent, semantic colors, theming.

Budget neutrals by product type: 3 to 5 neutrals for a landing page; for a product, about four background layers, at least one stroke (often two) and about three text colors, before hover and interactive states.
values: at least one stroke, often two

results.rule: Make the app frame or sidebar a slightly darker anchor than the main content, keeping the shift very small, especially in light mode (for example a 2% blue tint).
Define card edges on a light background with a border of roughly 85% white; do not use a thin black border.
Make buttons darker the more important they are, from ghost buttons up to black buttons with white text, with everything else in between.
Set text colors by importance: reserve the darkest (about 11% white) for important headings, most body text at 15 to 20% white, subtext at 30 to 40%.
Build the accent as a full ramp from lightest to darkest and assign steps by job: main color at 500 or 600, hover at 700, links at 400 or 500.
Do not derive dark mode by reflecting the light palette; roughly double the lightness distance between neutral steps (about 2% apart in light becomes four to 6% in dark).
In dark mode, move the primary brand color to step 300 or 400 with hover at 400 or 500, dim the text and brighten the borders.
In dark mode, make raised surfaces lighter than what they sit on, or give them only a border (like a search bar).
Always include semantic colors for states such as success, failure and in progress, even when the brand is black and white.
Make destructive actions red regardless of the brand color.
Build chart colors in OKLCH: fix lightness and chroma, then step the hue by about 25 to 30 for each series, instead of using neutrals or only the brand ramp.
Do not fill a site with endless pop-ups, paywalls in front of content or premium subscriptions that add nothing.
Give every intrusive feature a visible way to turn it off: a button beside it or a switch in settings.
When a feature blocks the user with a modal, include a notice in it that explains how to turn the feature off.
Do not use a modal that blocks every other action until the user finishes a chore such as naming a layer.
Do not shame users about how much they use the product (videos watched, time spent browsing), especially when the only choices offered are an upsell or continued notifications.
Do not write guilt-tripping or passive-aggressive messages about a user's progress, such as telling them they would need to run a marathon today to hit their step goal.
Do not pair a progress warning with a button that suggests the user change their goal.
Do not lock a web app to one browser or make users watch an ad to get access.
Do not put a paywall or an account requirement in front of simple content such as a recipe.
Do not punish users for breaking a streak, for example by making them guess where they were in a book.
Use signifiers so the UI explains itself: wrap related items in a shared container, put a container on the selected item, and gray out inactive items.
Give interactive elements signifiers such as a button press state, highlights on active nav items, hover states and tooltips.
Put the most important item at the top, large and bold, and place secondary details such as time and date below it, much smaller.
Add an image to cards whenever possible.
Don't treat a 12-column grid and exact eight-pixel spacing as laws; let custom layouts such as landing pages sit off the columns.
Prioritize white space, letting things breathe, over excessive grids and layouts.

In a simple section, put 32 pixels between every item, and group elements that just go together, such as the announcement and text or the text and subtext; grouped elements sit closer than 32 pixels [inferred]
Use a four-point grid: make every spacing value a multiple of four.
Use one font for the whole design: pick a nice sans serif and stick to it, without spending lots of time on the choice.
Tighten large header text: letter spacing by about -2% to -3%, and drop line height to about 110% to 120%.
On landing pages and websites, use no more than six font sizes; the range between them can be large.
On dashboards, shrink the type range so text sizes are normally not larger than 24 pixels.
Start the palette from one primary color, usually the brand color; lighten it for backgrounds and darken it for text colors.
Use semantic colors with fixed meanings: blue for trust, red for danger or urgency, yellow for warning, green for success.
Don't use color only as decoration; give it a purpose, such as an announcement bar that grabs attention, a focus state on an input, or a green 'new' chip on a link.
In dark mode, lower the contrast of light card borders.
In dark mode, create depth by making cards lighter than the background instead of relying on shadows.
In dark mode, dim the saturation and brightness of bright chips, and flip that treatment for the chip text.
Soften shadows by reducing their opacity and increasing their blur.
Match shadow strength to the layer: light shadows for cards, stronger shadows for content that sits above other content, such as popovers.
Don't let a shadow be the first thing people notice in a design.
Size icons to the line height of your font (24 pixels in the example), then tighten up the text.
Give every button at least four states: default, hovered, active or pressed, and disabled; add a loading state with a spinner when needed.
Give inputs a focus state when the user clicks in, error states with red borders and messages when something is wrong, and warning states for optional issues where needed.
Make every user action produce a response: loading spinners while data fetches, success messages when an action completes, micro animations on scroll or swipe.
Confirm an action with a micro interaction, for example a chip that slides up after the copy button is clicked.
Don't cover an image with a full-screen overlay just to make text readable.
For text over an image, add a linear gradient that shows the image and then smoothly converges into a text-readable background.
When cards sit on top of a dark background, place the rectangles very close to one another and keep the spacing between them precise.
Put a gradient under text that sits on a photo.
Pick images for thin photo bands and multi-image layouts with their crop, aspect ratio and orientation in mind.
In a giant-text hero, make the headline massive and the navbar text very small, and place the navbar beneath the headline.
Use a large, high-resolution photo when an image is blown up to fill a hero or section.
Do not make small navigation buttons the only way to move through a horizontal card carousel; add a bigger button or make the cards draggable with the mouse.
Keep a horizontal card carousel to 3 to about 10 cards; above 10, consider a different format.
Expect to resize and re-split bento boxes as the content plan takes shape, and let the content decide the layout.
values: three boxes instead of just two

results.rule: Only use a bento layout when you have enough content, whether text, images or both, to fill every box.
For a cut-out lettering effect over an image, choose an image that fits the space and has nothing important in the top corner that the cut-out would remove.
Give the body text in a text-only section three or more lines.
Use an ease-out curve as the default easing for most animations. Read with the rule on built-in easings, this means a custom ease-out curve rather than the built-in `ease-out` keyword [inferred].
Never make an animation longer than 1s unless it is illustrative.
Keep most animation durations around 0.2s to 0.3s.
Do not use CSS's built-in easing keywords other than `ease` and `linear`.
Use each easing curve for its described use case.
When an animation feels off but you cannot tell why, record it and play it back frame by frame.
Do not ship AI-generated motion just because it works; review it, name what is wrong and fix it.
Train motion judgement by comparing two animations side by side, picking the better one and writing down why before reading an expert breakdown.
Explain motion choices with bad-versus-good examples side by side.
Give AI coding tools a rules or skill file containing your animation principles before asking them for motion work.
Do not put spring-driven interactive graph behaviour (useSpring and related hooks) on functional data charts such as stock charts; keep it for illustrations.
Set transform origins correctly before applying transforms to SVG elements.
Decide easing and duration as part of building every component, not only the implementation.
Choose the easing and the duration of every animation deliberately; do not treat them as afterthoughts to the code.
State which easing and duration you chose for an animation, and why.
Pick which properties to animate with performance in mind.
Decide whether an element should animate at all, and do not animate when it should not.
Plan an animation by thinking and talking through what it should do before writing code; then code, improve and iterate.
Let people touch and experience an animation through an interactive example, not only a description of it.
Get CSS animation fundamentals (transforms, transitions, keyframe animations) right before reaching for Motion, and know when and how to use each.
Check orchestration, the feeling conveyed, accessibility and performance when taking an animation from good to great.
Do not alternate text-left, image-right rows all the way down a landing page; vary the section layouts.
Use a stacked hero layout instead of a side-by-side hero.
Show the actual product (for example its dashboard) instead of stock images that have little to do with the product.
Zoom in on the important parts of the product dashboard to curate exactly what the viewer sees, and at the highest level craft the visual to show exactly what the product does.
Do not pair sharp-edged images with rounded-corner buttons on the same page.
Use one font throughout the landing page.
Build a clear typographic hierarchy through color and size.
Keep hero copy short and punchy; cut vague, long blocks of text.
Do not repeat the company name in the copy when it is already visible on screen.
Write feature copy about how the product helps the user, not only what it does.
Give the navigation menu hierarchy: make the sign-up action and the more important links (such as Product) stand out, for example with an outline on the most important buttons.
Balance the navigation bar, for example by centering the secondary links, instead of weighting everything to the right.
Give the hero call to action the same label as the top navigation call to action when both go to the same place.
Do not apply the accent color haphazardly to everything that will reasonably take it.
Do not rely largely on images to supply the page's color.
Let the color pops come from the product visuals, which allows neutral (white) buttons.
When moving between mega menu items, keep the menu open and slide the content left or right instead of fully closing and reopening it.
Design each section to lead into the next, for example fading out the dashboard to segue into the features, instead of stacking unrelated sections.
Before building an idea, decide deliberately whether it deserves to be built; the fact that AI can build it in minutes is not a reason to build it.
When choosing between directions, build option A and option B and compare them instead of only theorizing about them.
Validate a prototyped idea before shipping it; do not treat having built it as the validation.
Do not ship option A and option B just because building them took little effort; let validation and judgement, not the low cost, decide what ships.
Do not release apps or UI libraries that were generated without a thought behind them.
Remove friction that only makes work slow or messy, but keep the friction that forces judgement about what is worth building; treat that friction as a feature, not a bug.
Use clip-path (not width, height or extra wrapper elements) to hide and reveal parts of an element in animations, because it does not change layout.

Use the inset() shape for clip-path animations; inset(100%) (the article's shorthand for inset(100%, 100%, 100%, 100%)) hides the whole element and inset(0 0 0 0) shows all of it. Write the values space-separated, as the article's code does (its comma form in prose is not valid CSS [inferred]).
Build before/after comparison sliders by overlaying the two images and clipping the top one with clip-path: inset(0 50% 0 0), updating the right inset from the drag position.
Do not build comparison (before and after) sliders by changing the width of overflow-hidden divs; clip one of two overlaid elements with clip-path instead.
Reveal images by starting at clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0) and animating to inset(0 0 0 0) over 1s (duration 1000 in the WAAPI version) with cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) and fill forwards.
Do not animate an image's height to reveal it; animate clip-path instead.
Trigger reveal animations such as the image reveal when the element enters the viewport.
If Framer Motion is not already in the project, detect viewport entry with the Intersection Observer API instead of adding Framer Motion.
Fire scroll-triggered reveals only once, and only after a meaningful part of the element is visible: with useInView use { once: true, margin: "-100px" }.
Measure scroll progress for a reveal with offset ["start end", "end end"] (from the element's top reaching the viewport bottom until its bottom reaches the viewport bottom).
Map scroll progress 0 to 1 onto the clip inset 100% to 0% (useTransform(scrollYProgress, [0, 1], ["100%", "0%"])) and apply it as inset(0 0 ${clipPathY} 0).
Keep scroll-driven values as motion values end to end (compose them with useMotionTemplate) and pass them as inline style; do not copy them into a plain const.
Do not rely on a text-colour transition to show the active tab changing.

Animate tab changes by duplicating the tab list, styling the duplicate as active (blue background, white text), clipping it to the active tab with a rounded inset (e.g. inset(0px 75% 0px 0% round 17px)), and animating that clip-path on click.
Hide the duplicated decorative layer from assistive technology and keyboard focus, as the author's code does: aria-hidden on the overlay container and tabIndex={-1} on its buttons.
In production, build clip-path tabs on an accessible tabs primitive such as Radix Tabs rather than the simplified demo.
Polish small interaction details such as tab transitions even when most users will not notice them.
Prefer the View Transitions API over duplicating the whole page or element for a theme-switch reveal.
Use ease-out, not ease-in, for enter animations.
Prefer a semi-transparent shadow over a solid border in UIs (the README gives no narrower scope or values).
Pick the library for a task from libraries the author uses and trusts, instead of letting an agent hand-roll a component such as a toast or install an abandoned package.
When building an animation from scratch, explicitly choose its curve, duration and properties.
Add motion only where it genuinely benefits the UI, and state explicitly what should not be animated.
Review animations strictly against the author's rules.
When auditing a codebase's animations, produce prioritized, self-contained plans that any agent can execute.
Describe an animation to an AI with its exact term rather than a vague description.
When a web app runs on a phone, fix sticky hover states, tap highlight flashes, the 100vh bug, inputs that zoom the page, laggy taps and safe areas.
In React Native and Expo, hold gestures, sheets, haptics and screen transitions to the same bar as the other animation skills, and keep motion off the JS thread.
Keep developing real design or engineering expertise and use AI to amplify it, not to replace it.
On mobile, move every hover affordance into press, position, or nothing; redesign it rather than porting it from the web.
Keep every React Native animation on the UI runtime (worklets), never on the React Native runtime.
Treat interruptibility and velocity handoff as the baseline for anything a finger touches, not as polish.
When building motion, make the call, state the reasoning in one line and write the code; do not present motion options as a menu.
Do not animate something that should not animate; the gate may correctly produce zero lines of code.
Never drive an animation with a setState per frame, a PanResponder or an animated height.
Run the build sequence in order; steps 1 (should it animate) and 2 (what is the purpose) gate everything else.
Use Reanimated, not React Native's core Animated.
Take curves and spring configs from the skill's tables; never approximate values.
Ship reduced-motion support with the animation, not as a follow-up.
Judge animation feel only on a release build on the slowest device you support.
Do not animate interactions seen 100+ times a day (tab switches, keyboard open/close, scrolling, settings toggles); use the platform default or nothing.
For interactions seen tens of times a day (press feedback, list navigation, row selection), use only near-imperceptible motion under 150ms, or nothing.
Give occasional elements (sheets, modals, toasts, onboarding steps) standard animation.
Spend the delight budget only on rare or first-time moments (success states, empty-state illustrations, celebration).
Never slide between tabs; set animation: 'none'.
If a requested animation fails the frequency gate, say so and don't write it.

Name the purpose of each animation in one word before building it: feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation, or delight (rare tier only); if you can't name it, don't build it.
Pick the cheapest tool that works by walking down the tool table and stopping at the first that fits.
Use a Reanimated CSS transition (transitionProperty in the style) for a state-driven change with no gesture: press, toggle, color, a value flipping.
Use a Reanimated CSS animation (animationName keyframes) for loops, multi-stage motion, or motion that plays on mount with no state change.
Use layout animations (entering / exiting / itemLayoutAnimation) for elements mounting or unmounting and for list reflow.
Use useSharedValue + Gesture + useAnimatedStyle for anything a finger touches or anything derived from scroll.
Use native stack options in Expo Router for screen-to-screen transitions; never hand-roll them.
Use presentation: 'formSheet' for a bottom sheet that is its own screen.
Use NativeTabs (from expo-router/unstable-native-tabs) for the tab bar.
Use Link.Menu / Link.Preview (Expo Router) for context menus and press-and-hold previews; never rebuild them in JS.
For a header that collapses into a large title, use headerLargeTitleEnabled on the native stack, not a scroll worklet.
Use RefreshControl for pull to refresh; hand-roll it only when it is a signature interaction.
Use react-native-keyboard-controller for UI that tracks the keyboard.
Use Lottie only for vector illustration, celebration and empty states; never for UI state.
Reach for a shared value only when the value is continuous or interruptible: a press scale is a CSS transition, a drag is a shared value.
Install motion packages with npx expo install <package>, not plain npm install.

Use react-native-reanimated + react-native-worklets for animation, react-native-gesture-handler for gestures, expo-router for navigation, sheets, native tabs and menus, expo-haptics for haptics, react-native-keyboard-controller (with KeyboardProvider at the root) for keyboard-following UI, lottie-react-native for illustration, and @shopify/react-native-skia for very large scenes.
Animate only transform and opacity; do not animate width, height, margin, padding, flex, top, left or gap (the one exception is an absolutely positioned element with no children).
When an absolutely positioned element with no children (a tab pill, a progress bar fill) has to change size, animate its width rather than scaleX; it is the only exception to transform and opacity.
Never enter from scale(0); start from scale(0.9–0.97) plus opacity: 0.
Put translate before scale in a React Native transform array unless you want the translate multiplied.
On Android, never animate elevation; animate the opacity of a pre-shadowed layer instead.
Never animate BlurView intensity; crossfade the opacity of a static BlurView instead.
If a finger was involved, use a spring; use timing for everything else.
Configure Reanimated springs with duration and dampingRatio (Apple's two designer parameters), not mass/stiffness/damping.
Use { duration: 400, dampingRatio: 1 } for a default settle with no overshoot.
Use { duration: 400, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity } to reposition or snap back after a drag.
Use { duration: 300, dampingRatio: 0.8, velocity } for sheets and drawers.
Add overshootClamping: true to any spring that must not pass a hard edge.
Allow bounce (overshoot) only when the gesture carried momentum.
Use ease-out for elements entering or exiting, and as the default easing.
Use ease-in-out for elements moving or morphing on screen.
Use linear easing for constant motion such as progress and marquees.
Never use ease-in (Easing.in(...)) on a UI element.
Do not use Reanimated's built-in easings; use custom bezier curves instead.
Use Easing.bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) as the strong ease-out for UI.
Use Easing.bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) for on-screen movement.
Use Easing.bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) as the iOS sheet curve.
Give press feedback a duration of 100–150ms.
Give toggles, chips and small state changes a duration of 150–200ms.
Animate sheets, modals and drawers with a spring of about 300ms perceived duration.
Use the platform default duration for screen transitions; don't override it.
Keep mobile UI animations under 300ms, the same as web; match the platform only for navigation (iOS push is 350ms) and beat it everywhere else.
Never call setState from a gesture or scroll handler; drive the style from a shared value through useAnimatedStyle.
Never call scheduleOnRN inside onUpdate or a scroll handler; call it in onEnd, or in a useAnimatedReaction that fires when a value crosses a threshold.
Use scheduleOnRN(fn, ...args) from react-native-worklets instead of the deprecated runOnJS(fn)(...args).
Never read a shared value during render (for example translateY.get() in JSX).
Never write a shared value during render; touch shared values only in worklets, handlers and effects.
Access shared values with .get() / .set(), not .value; use the functional form sv.set((v) => v + 1) for updates based on the current value.
Put 'worklet' as the first line of any function called from a worklet.
Show feedback on press-in and commit the action on press-out.
Scale every pressable to 0.97 in 100–150ms, using Pressable plus a CSS transition.
Make touch targets at least 44×44pt on iOS.
Make touch targets at least 48dp on Android.
When the visual is smaller than the minimum target, add hitSlop instead of growing the visual.
Set pressRetentionOffset on pressables.
Use the Android ripple only in a Material-styled app; in a custom-designed app use the same press scale on both platforms.
Fire Haptics.selectionAsync() when a value ticks past a step: picker, slider detent, segmented control.
Fire Haptics.impactAsync(ImpactFeedbackStyle.Light) when something snaps home, a sheet detent catches, or a drag commits.
Fire Haptics.impactAsync(ImpactFeedbackStyle.Medium) when a heavy object lands or a destructive action fires.
Fire Haptics.notificationAsync(NotificationFeedbackType.Success / Error) when an operation succeeds or fails.
Fire a haptic in the same frame as its visual, at the causal moment (the detent catching), not when the animation finishes.
Use at most one haptic per user action: never on scroll, never per frame, never on an entrance animation the user didn't cause.
Never make a haptic the only feedback; always pair it with a visual that stands alone.
From a worklet, schedule haptics back to the React Native runtime, e.g. scheduleOnRN(Haptics.selectionAsync).
Read reduced motion with useReducedMotion(), or pass reduceMotion: ReduceMotion.System to each animation.
Under reduced motion, keep opacity and color changes that explain a state change and drop translation, scale, parallax and overshoot.
Under reduced motion, switch screen transitions to animation: 'fade'.
Never animate to a hardcoded height; measure with onLayout, or animate a transform instead.

Install Reanimated through Expo (npx expo install react-native-reanimated react-native-worklets) and rely on babel-preset-expo for the worklets Babel plugin; in a bare React Native project without that preset, add the plugin manually and last in the list.
When using react-native-keyboard-controller for keyboard-following UI, put KeyboardProvider at the root.
Wrap the app in GestureHandlerRootView.
Run the app on the New Architecture when using Reanimated 4.
Never judge animation feel in Expo Go, a dev build or the simulator; use a release build on the slowest supported device.
Confirm CADisableMinimumFrameDurationOnPhone is true in expo.ios.infoPlist, and add it if missing.

When a request matches a recipe (press feedback, drag-to-dismiss sheet, swipe-to-delete, collapsing header, list entrances, keyboard-synced UI, tab indicator, screen transitions), start from the recipe rather than a blank file.
Never use PanResponder; use Gesture.Pan() from gesture-handler.
Never use core Animated for anything a finger touches; use Reanimated.
Never put entering on a virtualized list row; animate the container, or use itemLayoutAnimation.
Never rebuild a screen transition in JS; use the native stack animation option.
Never use a distance-only dismissal threshold; dismiss on velocity or distance, so a flick is enough.
Never hard-stop an element at a boundary; apply rubber-band resistance.

After writing motion code, report in a few lines: the gate result (frequency tier, named purpose, and what was rejected and why), the ingredients (tool, properties, spring or curve plus duration, thread), and what to feel-check on device (flick it, interrupt it mid-flight, reverse it, run it on the slowest Android).
Do not pad the motion deliverable into a report; the code is the deliverable.
Say it plainly when the honest answer is that something shouldn't animate, or that it needs a real device before its feel can be judged.
Start from the matching recipe and adapt it; do not rebuild common animations from scratch.
Write the recipes' curves as the --ease-out, --ease-in-out and --ease-drawer tokens defined in SKILL.md, referenced with var().
Give every pressable element press feedback: transition: transform 160ms var(--ease-out) and transform: scale(0.97) on :active.
Apply the press scale to the whole button so the label and icons scale with it.
Leave the :active press ungated, and gate any :hover styling separately.
Scale dropdowns, popovers, menus, selects and tooltips out of their trigger with transform-origin: var(--transform-origin).

Transition dropdown, popover, menu and select opacity and transform over 200ms var(--ease-out), entering from and exiting to opacity: 0 and transform: scale(0.95) ([data-starting-style] and [data-ending-style]).
Transition tooltip transform and opacity over 125ms var(--ease-out), entering from and exiting to opacity: 0 and transform: scale(0.97).
Keep an initial delay before the first tooltip opens.
Once one tooltip is open, open neighbouring tooltips instantly by skipping both the delay and the animation (transition-duration: 0ms on [data-instant]).
Keep modals centered with transform-origin: center; they are exempt from the trigger origin.
Transition modal opacity and transform over 250ms var(--ease-out), entering from and exiting to opacity: 0 and transform: scale(0.96).
Fade the modal backdrop's opacity alongside the modal with the same timing (opacity 250ms var(--ease-out)).
Animate drawers and sheets with transform: translateY(0) when open and translateY(100%) when closed ([data-closed]), over 500ms var(--ease-drawer).
When a drawer can be dragged, treat it as a gesture and follow the drag-to-dismiss recipe.
Animate toasts in from opacity: 0 and translateY(100%) using @starting-style, transitioning opacity and transform over 400ms ease.
Use ease rather than ease-out for toasts and run them slightly slower than typical UI, tuning motion to the component's personality.
Where @starting-style is not available, fall back to a mount flag (useEffect(() => { setMounted(true); }, []) with data-mounted={mounted}).
When stacked toasts reflow, adjust the opacity change against the height change by feel, then check it again the next day.
Animate accordions with overflow: hidden and height and opacity over 200ms var(--ease-out).
Keep accordion animations short.
Do not animate height to auto; measure the content height in JS, or use a headless primitive that supplies it.

Stagger a group entrance: each item starts at opacity: 0 and transform: translateY(8px) and runs animation: fadeIn 300ms var(--ease-out) forwards to opacity: 1 and translateY(0), with animation-delay 50ms, 100ms and 150ms on the 2nd, 3rd and 4th items.
Do not stagger a list the user scrolls past all day; keep stagger for lists or grids seen occasionally.
Never let a stagger block interaction while it plays.
Use hold-to-confirm for destructive actions where a plain click is too easy to fire by accident.

Build hold-to-confirm with an overlay clipped by clip-path: inset(0 100% 0 0) that fills to inset(0 0 0 0) over 2s linear while the button is :active, snaps back over 200ms var(--ease-out) on release, and scale(0.97) on the button while pressed.
Use linear easing for progress fills.

For a tab indicator with a colour change, do not time individual colour transitions; duplicate the tab list, style the copy as the active state (different background and text colour), clip the copy so only the active tab shows, and animate the clip.
Animate the active tab copy's clip-path (driven by the active tab's position) over 250ms var(--ease-in-out).
Use scroll reveals only on marketing surfaces, never on functional UI a user visits daily.
Build scroll reveals by transitioning clip-path from inset(0 0 100% 0) to inset(0 0 0 0) over 600ms var(--ease-in-out) when [data-visible] is set.
Trigger scroll reveals with IntersectionObserver or Motion's useInView with { once: true, margin: "-100px" }, and fire them only once.
Use springs, not durations, for drag-to-dismiss.
Dismiss a dragged element on a flick as well as on distance: compute velocity = Math.abs(swipeAmount) / timeTaken and dismiss when Math.abs(swipeAmount) >= SWIPE_THRESHOLD or velocity > 0.11.
Set the dragged element's transform directly (element.style.transform = `translateY(${distance}px)`) rather than through a CSS variable on the parent.
Capture the pointer once a drag starts.
Ignore new touch points while a drag is in progress (if (isDragging) return).
Damp dragging past a natural boundary so the element moves less the further it goes.
Allow over-drag with rising resistance instead of stopping it at a hard wall.
Settle a released or interrupted drag with a spring, { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }, not a duration.
Keep blur under 20px.
When motion needs JS control but not a dependency, use WAAPI (element.animate()), for example a clip-path reveal with { duration: 1000, fill: 'forwards', easing: 'cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)' }.
Do not animate an element when motion would not serve it; treat producing no animation code as a successful outcome.
Make the motion call yourself, state the reasoning in one line and write the code instead of presenting motion options as a menu.
Run the build sequence in order, and settle steps 1 (should it animate) and 2 (purpose) before choosing any curve.
Take every curve, duration and spring config from the skill's tables; never invent or approximate one such as cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1) because it looks familiar.
Use the codebase's existing motion tokens (for example --ease-out or an existing duration scale) and extend them instead of adding a parallel system.
Ship the reduced-motion variant and hover gating in the same change as the animation, never as a follow-up.
Use the cheapest tool that works; do not install a motion library for a fade.
Never animate actions performed 100+ times a day, such as keyboard shortcuts or toggling a command palette.
For elements used tens of times a day (hover effects, list navigation), use only near-imperceptible motion that is fast and subtle, or none.
Give occasional elements such as modals, drawers and toasts standard animation.
Spend the delight budget only on rare or first-time moments such as onboarding, success and celebration.
Do not animate keyboard-initiated actions.
When a request fails the frequency gate, say so plainly, do not write the animation, and offer a non-motion alternative such as an instant state change or a static affordance.
Name the animation's purpose as one of feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation or delight before building it; if none fits, do not build it.
Do not add motion to a frequently seen element because it looks cool.
Use explanatory animation (demonstrating how something works) only on marketing and onboarding surfaces.
Do not move data the user is reading or acting on for style; keep decorative effects such as mouse-tracking on marketing pages, not on functional views like a graph in a banking app.
Use a CSS transition for hover, press, color and state toggles controlled by a class or attribute.
Use CSS @starting-style for entry animations on mount that need no JS state.
Use a CSS animation for predetermined motion that must stay smooth while the page is busy loading.
Use WAAPI (element.animate()) when you need programmatic control with CSS performance and no library.
Reserve the Motion library (motion.dev) for springs, layout animations, exit animations and gesture-driven values.
Use CSS for predetermined motion and JS for dynamic and interruptible motion.

When the task needs a component (toast, drawer, command menu, dropdown) rather than an animation, stop and choose a UI library (the source invokes its pick-ui-library skill) instead of hand-rolling it.
Animate only transform and opacity; do not animate width, height, margin, padding, top or left.
Treat clip-path as the only sanctioned fourth animatable property, and animate height only for accordions.
Never start an entrance from scale(0); start from scale(0.9-0.97) with opacity: 0.
Set transform-origin at the trigger for popovers, dropdowns, menus and tooltips (var(--transform-origin) in Base UI), and keep modals centered.
Use percentages in translate() (for example translateY(100%)) rather than hardcoded pixels.
In Motion, animate with the full transform string (for example transform: "translateX(100px)") instead of the x, y or scale shorthands.
Set transform on the animated element directly; never drive a child's transform from a CSS variable on the parent.
Use ease-out for elements entering or exiting, and as the default.
Use ease-in-out for elements moving or morphing on screen.
Use ease for hover and color changes.
Use linear for constant motion such as a marquee or progress.
Never use ease-in on a UI element.

Define and use strong custom curves instead of built-in CSS easings: --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) for UI, --ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) for on-screen movement, --ease-drawer: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) for iOS-like drawers.
Do not use the built-in ease-out keyword on a deliberate animation; use cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1).
When a curve is needed that is not in the table, take it from easing.dev or easings.co; do not hand-roll one.
Give button press feedback a duration of 100-160ms.
Give tooltips and small popovers a duration of 125-200ms.
Give dropdowns and selects a duration of 150-250ms.
Give modals and drawers a duration of 200-500ms.
Keep UI animations under 300ms; without a reason, use 150-250ms.
Use a spring instead of a duration for drag with momentum, elements that should feel alive, gestures the user can interrupt or reverse, and decorative mouse-tracking.
Configure springs as { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 } (Apple-style) or { type: "spring", mass: 1, stiffness: 100, damping: 10 } (traditional physics).
Keep spring bounce between 0.1 and 0.3, avoid bounce in most UI, and reserve it for drag-to-dismiss and playful interactions.
Use CSS transitions, not keyframes, for toasts, toggles and anything a user can fire twice in a second.
Use springs for gestures.
Exit the way it entered: an element that slides in from the bottom leaves through the bottom.
Use asymmetric timing where the user is deciding: slow on the deliberate phase (hold-to-confirm press 2s linear), snappy on the system response (release 200ms ease-out).
Under @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce), keep opacity and color animation (for example animation: fade 0.2s ease) and drop transform-based motion.
Do not remove all animation for reduced motion; keep transitions that aid comprehension and remove movement and position changes.
In React, read useReducedMotion() and swap movement values for static ones (for example closedX = reduce ? 0 : '-100%').
Gate hover motion behind @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine); never ship ungated :hover motion.
Start from the matching recipe (button press, dropdown, tooltip, modal, drawer, toast, accordion, stagger, hold-to-confirm, tab indicator, scroll reveal, drag-to-dismiss) instead of a blank file.
Never use transition: all; name the exact properties being transitioned.
Do not bring every element in at once; stagger group entrances by 30-80ms.
Self-check the finished animation against the Never Ship list before finishing.

After writing the code, report in a few lines the gate result (frequency tier, named purpose, anything rejected and why) and the ingredients (tool, properties, curve, duration or spring config), one line each.

When a result depends on feel that cannot be judged from code (a crossfade, a spring's bounce, the opacity/height balance in an entering list), say so and point to the check: play it at 2-5x duration or in the DevTools animation inspector, step it frame by frame, test gestures on a real device, and look again the next day.
Do not pad the output into a report; keep the explanation to a few lines after the code.
Build every animation so it passes a strict review (the review-animations bar) the first time.

Keep an animation-building task to construction: send codebase audits to improve-animations, diff critiques to review-animations, hunting for places that could animate to find-animation-opportunities, and React Native work to animate-expo.
Avoid the wrong ingredients even when the element should animate: ease-in on an entrance, scale(0), keyframes on a toast, or a duration that makes a dropdown feel sluggish.

When first invoked without a specific question, the animate skill replies only with its one-line readiness statement and gives no other information until the user asks (this skill's own agent behaviour).
Keep the tone opinionated and brief, and give the honest answer 'this shouldn't animate' when it applies.
Put app-wide toast defaults in the Toaster's toastOptions and override them per toast() call; per-call options win over toastOptions.
Show at most 3 toasts at once by default (visibleToasts).
Place toasts bottom-right by default, choosing only from top-left, top-center, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-center or bottom-right.
Offset the toaster 32px from the screen edges on desktop.
Use a smaller 16px edge offset when the screen is narrower than 600px (mobileOffset).
Let swipe-to-dismiss directions follow the toaster position, and set swipeDirections only when they must differ.
Keep a keyboard shortcut that moves focus to the toaster area, Alt+T by default.
Space expanded toasts with a gap of 14 by default.
Auto-close toasts after 4000 ms by default.
Leave toasts dismissible by the user; set dismissible: false only when the user must not be able to close it.
Give a toast a custom id when it will be updated later, and call toast() again with that id to update it instead of adding a new toast.
When more than one Toaster exists, give each an id and send each toast to one with toasterId.
Style individual toast parts with classNames (toast, title, description, actionButton, cancelButton, closeButton) and mark those classes !important unless the toast is unstyled.
values: { toast, title, description, actionButton, cancelButton, closeButton }

results.rule: Handle manual closes in onDismiss and timeouts in onAutoClose; they are different events.
Keep an ARIA label on the toast container, 'Notifications' by default, and localise it with containerAriaLabel.
Use toast.success, toast.error, toast.info and toast.warning for status messages so each gets its matching icon.
Use toast.promise(promise, { loading, success, error }) for async work, where success and error can be strings, JSX, functions of the result, or objects of toast options.
Mount one <Toaster /> once, as close to the root as possible (several toasters are a separate recipe, each with its own id).
In Next.js, put the Toaster in layout.tsx.
Never render the Toaster per page or conditionally.
Call toast() only from client code (event handlers, effects, callbacks); it is a plain function, so no hook or provider is needed.
Do not call toast() inside a server action; return the result and call toast() in the client code that receives it.
Import Toaster once, in the layout, and import toast wherever client code needs it.
For a plain message use toast('Title') and add { description } for a second line.
For success, error, info or warning messages use the typed calls toast.success, toast.error, toast.info and toast.warning.
When you manage the async state yourself, show toast.loading('…') and then update that toast by its id.

When the loading, success and error states are tied to one promise, use toast.promise(promise, { loading, success, error }), passing functions to success and error to use the resolved value or the error.
Give a toast a button that does something with { action: { label, onClick } }, use cancel for the secondary button, and call event.preventDefault() in onClick to keep the toast open.
For custom JSX with no default styles at all, use toast.custom((t) => <jsx />) and use t's id to dismiss it.
Update a toast by calling toast() again with the same id, passing only the props that change; switch its type with a typed call such as toast.success(…, { id }).
With more than one Toaster, give each an id and target it with toasterId in every toast() call.
Handle onDismiss and onAutoClose separately, and wire both when you need to react to every way a toast closes.
Climb the styling ladder (defaults, inline style, classNames, headless) only as far as the change requires; jumping straight to headless is fine.
Do not settle on the middle styling rungs (inline styles or !important classes) as the long-term setup.
Start from the defaults, adding richColors on the Toaster for colorful success and error, and invert to flip toasts against the theme.
When styling toast parts with classNames (toast, title, description, actionButton, cancelButton, closeButton), mark every class !important; in Tailwind use the ! prefix.
Once more than a few classes need !important, stop and go headless.
Build the design-system toast headless with toast.custom() and your own JSX, and wrap it in your own toast() abstraction.
Prefer headless toast.custom() over unstyled: true.
Set the Toaster theme to 'system' or pass your theme provider's resolved theme, e.g. <Toaster theme={resolvedTheme} /> from next-themes.
If a toast never appears, check that a Toaster is mounted at the root and not unmounted by a conditional render or per-page placement, and that toast() runs on the client.
Do not mount a Toaster in both the layout and a page; keep one.
Fire toasts from event handlers rather than effects, or pass a stable id when a toast must fire from an effect.
When toasts render completely unstyled (common in Astro and with view transitions), import the stylesheet explicitly in a layout.
Inside Shadow DOM, copy the style tag whose text includes [data-sonner-toaster] into the shadow root.
Mount the Toaster at the document root, outside any dialog or portal container, so toasts are not hidden behind modals or clipped.
Do not place the Toaster inside an element that uses transform, filter or overflow [inferred].
Add richColors to the Toaster when success and error must look green and red.
If a toast never closes, check for duration: Infinity, dismissible: false, or a toast.promise whose promise never settles.
Pass toast.promise a promise, or a function returning one, that actually resolves or rejects.
If swipe-to-dismiss goes the wrong way or does not work, override swipeDirections on the Toaster.
Keep toasts off the screen edge with offset on desktop (default 32px) and mobileOffset below 600px (default 16px), as numbers, CSS strings or per-side objects.
Answer Sonner tasks from the skill first, and read API.md when an exact prop name, type or default is needed.
When Tailwind or CSS classes on toasts have no effect, mark them !important or move to unstyled or headless.
Give every animation a stated purpose: spatial consistency, state indication, feedback, explanation, or preventing a jarring change.
Do not accept 'it looks cool' as the purpose for an animation on a frequently seen element.
Do not animate anything used 100+ times a day, such as keyboard shortcuts and the command palette toggle.
Remove or drastically reduce animation on elements used tens of times a day, such as hover effects and list navigation.
Use standard animation for occasional UI such as modals, drawers and toasts.
Do not give keyboard-initiated actions or command palettes an open/close transition.
Do not put decorative motion on list items or hover states that are hit constantly; consider deleting the animation first.
Use ease-out for elements entering or exiting.
Use ease-in-out for elements moving or morphing on screen.
Use ease for hover and color changes.
Use linear only for constant motion such as marquees and progress.
Default to ease-out when no other easing case applies.
Never use ease-in on UI animation.
Do not use bare ease or linear on entrances.
For deliberate motion, introduce strong custom curves as tokens that match the repo's conventions instead of relying on built-in CSS easings.
Define the strong UI ease-out token as --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1).
Define the on-screen movement token as --ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1).
Define the drawer token as --ease-drawer: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1).
Keep UI animations under 300ms; durations over 300ms on UI elements are findings.
Set button press feedback duration to 100-160ms.
Set tooltip and small popover durations to 125-200ms.
Set dropdown and select durations to 150-250ms.
Set modal and drawer durations to 200-500ms.
In a toolbar, give only the first tooltip its delay and animation; show subsequent tooltips instantly.
Copy target values from the playbook exactly; never approximate them.
Never animate from scale(0); start entrances from scale(0.9-0.97) combined with opacity: 0.
Do not use pure-fade entrances with no initial transform.
Scale popovers, dropdowns and tooltips from their trigger, not from center, using transform-origin: var(--transform-origin).
Keep modals centered with transform-origin: center and do not report it as a finding.
Give pressable elements press feedback: transform: scale(0.97) on :active with transition: transform 160ms ease-out.
Keep press-feedback scale subtle, between 0.95 and 0.98.
Use CSS transitions or springs, not keyframes, for anything triggered rapidly or reversible mid-motion (stacking toasts, toggles, drags, expand/collapse).
Do not use @keyframes on toasts, toggles or other rapidly triggered UI.
Animate entry without JS using @starting-style; use a data-mounted attribute set in useEffect as the legacy fallback.
Drive gesture-driven motion with springs, not fixed-duration keyframe tweens.
Use the Apple-style spring config { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 } as the recommended default.
Keep spring bounce subtle at 0.1-0.3, and reserve visible bounce for drag-to-dismiss and playful moments.
Use asymmetric timing: animate deliberate phases (press, hold, destructive confirm) slower and make the system's response snap.
Dismiss drags by velocity (Math.abs(distance)/elapsedMs > ~0.11), not by distance thresholds alone.
Apply rising friction at drag boundaries instead of hard stops.
Animate only transform and opacity; never animate width, height, margin, padding, top or left.
Never use transition: all; list the exact properties to transition.
In Framer Motion, animate the full transform string (animate={{ transform: "translateX(100px)" }}) instead of the x/y/scale shorthands.
Set transform directly on each animated element; do not drive child transforms through a CSS variable on the parent (e.g. setProperty('--x', ...)).
Use CSS or WAAPI for predetermined motion and JS/springs for dynamic and gesture-driven motion; do not run rAF loops for what CSS could do.
Keep transition-time filter: blur() under 20px.
Handle prefers-reduced-motion for every moving animation: keep opacity and color, drop movement (e.g. animation: fade 0.2s ease).
Do not remove all feedback under reduced motion; keep transitions that aid comprehension and remove position changes.
In JS, read useReducedMotion() and branch transform values on it.
Gate hover motion behind @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine).
Match motion to the product's personality (playful can be bouncier, a dashboard stays crisp) and keep it consistent across components.
Keep curves and durations as shared tokens and consolidate near-identical hand-typed cubic-beziers or durations.
Stagger group entrances (lists, grids) by 30-80ms instead of animating everything at once.
Never let a stagger block interaction.
Add a brief transition to state changes that teleport, such as content swaps and layout jumps.
Animate spatially connected UI, such as a panel that appears from a trigger, so the motion explains where it came from.
Use translate percentages (translateY(100%) equals the element's own height) and clip-path: inset() reveals instead of hardcoded pixel offsets.
Report at most a handful of missed opportunities, each grounded in a UX seam you actually observed.

Write every animation-fix plan in the fixed structure: a title line '# NNN — <Short imperative title>' followed by Status, Commit, Severity, Category and Estimated scope, then Problem, Target, Repo conventions to follow, Steps, Boundaries and Verification sections.
Write the plan so an executor with zero context and zero taste can complete it; the plan must contain everything, exactly.
Never refer back to earlier discussion such as 'the audit above' or 'the easing we discussed'.
Set a new plan's Status to TODO.
Stamp the Commit field with the output of git rev-parse --short HEAD at the time the plan is written.
Mark Severity as exactly one of HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW, and name the audit category.
State the estimated scope as the number of files and a rough size.
In Problem, say what is wrong, where, and why it matters to how the product feels.
Cite every problem location as path/to/file.tsx:123 and include the current code verbatim.
Label each code excerpt with a comment giving its location and whether it is the current or the target code, e.g. /* src/components/dropdown.css:14 — current */ and /* target */.
In Target, spell out the exact end state with every value: curves, durations, spring configs and media queries.
Never write a vague target such as 'use a nicer easing'.
Document how the codebase already handles the pattern (token names, file placement, prop patterns) and give one exemplar file:line for the executor to imitate.
values: <exemplar file:line that already does this correctly>

results.rule: Add new easing curves to the repo's existing token file rather than inline, e.g. --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) in src/styles/tokens.css.
Write Steps as one concrete edit per step: the file, what changes, and the resulting code.
List the files and components the executor must not touch.
Restrict the executor to motion properties; do not change markup or structure unless a step says so.
Do not add new dependencies in an animation-fix plan.
If a step does not match the code found (drift since the commit stamp), stop and report instead of improvising.
In Verification, give the exact mechanical commands (typecheck, lint, build) with their expected outcome.

Include a feel check: run the UI, trigger the interaction, and list observable checks such as 'the dropdown scales from its trigger, not from center' and 'spamming the toggle never restarts the animation from zero'.
In the feel check, set DevTools animation playback to 10% (Animations panel) and confirm the specific detail.
In the feel check, toggle prefers-reduced-motion (Rendering panel) and confirm movement is dropped but opacity feedback remains.
End Verification with 'Done when' criteria that a machine or an eye can check.
Write one plan per finding; merge two findings into one plan only when they share every file and the same fix pattern.
Pull every value from AUDIT.md; never approximate from memory.
Never skip the feel check; give the executor or reviewer concrete things to watch in slow motion.
After writing plans, create or update plans/README.md with a table of plans (number, title, severity, status), the recommended execution order and dependencies between plans.
Cite the exact values in this reference in review findings instead of approximating.
Do not animate actions used 100+ times a day, such as keyboard shortcuts and the command palette toggle.
Remove or drastically reduce animation on actions used tens of times a day, such as hover effects and list navigation.
Give occasional UI such as modals, drawers and toasts standard animation.
Never animate keyboard-initiated actions.
Animate only for a valid purpose: spatial consistency, state indication, explanation, feedback, or preventing a jarring change.
Do not justify motion on a frequently seen element with 'it looks cool'.
Use ease-out for elements entering or exiting.
Use ease-in-out for elements moving or morphing on screen.
Use ease for hover and color changes.
Use linear for constant motion such as marquees and progress.
Default to ease-out when no other easing case applies.
Never use ease-in on UI.
Use the strong custom curve cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) as the ease-out for UI instead of the built-in ease-out.
Use cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) as the ease-in-out for on-screen movement.
Use cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) for iOS-like drawers.
Find easing curves at easing.dev or easings.co instead of hand-rolling them from scratch.
Keep button press feedback at 100–160ms.
Keep tooltips and small popovers at 125–200ms.
Keep dropdowns and selects at 150–250ms.
Keep modals and drawers at 200–500ms.
Keep UI animations under 300ms.
Make loading spinners spin faster.
After the first tooltip in a toolbar has shown, show later tooltips instantly, skipping both the delay and the animation.
Never animate from scale(0); start from scale(0.9–0.97) with opacity: 0.
Scale popovers from their trigger with transform-origin: var(--transform-origin), not from center.
Keep modals at transform-origin: center.
Give every pressable element press feedback of transform: scale(0.97) on :active with transition: transform 160ms ease-out.
Keep press-feedback scale subtle, between 0.95 and 0.98.
Use springs for drag with momentum, 'alive' elements such as the Dynamic Island, interruptible gestures and decorative mouse tracking.
Prefer the Apple-style spring config { type: "spring", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }.
Keep spring bounce subtle, between 0.1 and 0.3.
Avoid bounce in most UI; reserve it for drag-to-dismiss and playful interactions.
Use springs for gestures users may reverse mid-motion.
For decorative mouse-following motion, interpolate with useSpring rather than tying the value directly to mouse position.
Do not spring-smooth mouse-tied motion unless the motion is decorative.
Use CSS transitions for anything triggered rapidly, such as toasts being added or toggles.
Avoid @keyframes animations for dynamic UI.
Use @starting-style for entry animations without JS.
Make motion slow where the user is deciding and fast where the system responds.
For a press-and-hold overlay (.button:active .overlay), run the press phase slow and linear and the release phase fast with ease-out.
Animate only transform and opacity.
Do not animate padding, margin, height, width, top or left.
Do not drive child transforms through a CSS variable on the parent; set transform directly on the element.
Use the full transform string in Framer Motion (animate={{ transform: "translateX(100px)" }}) instead of x/y/scale shorthands.
Use CSS for predetermined motion and JS for dynamic or interruptible motion.
Use WAAPI (element.animate) when you need JS control with CSS performance.
Move elements by their own size with translate percentages such as translateY(100%) rather than hardcoded pixels.
Dismiss swipeable elements by velocity: compute Math.abs(distance)/elapsedMs and dismiss if it exceeds about 0.11.
Do not require crossing a distance threshold to dismiss a swipe.
Damp drags past a natural edge so the element moves less the further you drag.
Capture the pointer once dragging starts.
Ignore extra touch points after a drag begins (if (isDragging) return).
Allow over-drag with rising resistance instead of an invisible hard stop.
When a crossfade still shows two overlapping states after tuning easing and duration, add filter: blur(2px) during the transition.
Keep animated blur under 20px.
Stagger group entrances with 30–80ms between items.
Do not use stagger delays longer than 30–80ms between items.
Never block interaction while a stagger plays.
Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, keep opacity and color animation and drop transform-based motion.
Gate hover motion behind @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine).
In React, read useReducedMotion and remove positional movement when it is on, for example closedX = reduce ? 0 : '-100%'.
Do not remove all animation for reduced motion; keep transitions that aid comprehension and remove movement and position changes.

Check motion feel in slow motion by raising duration 2–5× or using the DevTools animation inspector, verifying clean color crossfades, no abrupt easing stop, the right transform-origin, and coordinated properties staying in sync.
Step through animations frame by frame in the Chrome DevTools Animations panel to find timing drift between coordinated properties.
Test gestures such as drawers and swipes on real devices by connecting a phone, hitting the dev server by IP and using Safari remote devtools.
Review motion again with fresh eyes the next day.
Match motion to the component's personality: playful can be bouncier, a professional dashboard should be crisp and fast.

Check the project's Swift toolchain before applying this guidance: treat Swift 6.3 as the baseline, treat rows marked with the warning sign as unreleased Swift 6.4, and do not apply the Swift 6.2 rules about async and @concurrent to projects on Swift 6.1 or earlier.
Start with the simplest, most static, most single-threaded thing that works, and add concurrency, reference semantics, existentials or unsafe pointers only where you can point at the reason.

Move down the hierarchy of defaults only with a reason you can state: data starts as struct/enum, abstraction as a concrete type, polymorphism as some P, execution on the main actor synchronously, memory as Array/String, safety as a safe API.
Keep Array and String for memory until profiling shows the cost; only then reach for InlineArray or Span.
Use safe APIs by default; use Unsafe* only for C interop or a measured hot path.
Default to struct and enum; use class only for identity, shared mutable state, inheritance or resource lifetime.
Declare with let by default and use var only when you mutate.

Do not leave a struct with a mutable reference-type property as is: keep the referenced type immutable, expose only computed properties that forward to it, or make it a private stored property behind copy-on-write.
Implement copy-on-write by wrapping a final class in a struct and checking isKnownUniquelyReferenced(&storage) before mutating, copying first if it is not unique.
Model a fixed set of things and mutually exclusive state with an enum; replace piles of optional stored properties (isSharing, selectedRows, shareTarget) with one enum State.
Compose structs from value-type stored properties so the whole type has value semantics.
Use noncopyable types (~Copyable) for unique ownership such as a file descriptor, a bank transfer or an open resource, and mark the finishing method consuming.
Throw for recoverable errors; use precondition or fatalError for programmer mistakes.
Make error types enums with associated values that carry context, e.g. case duplicateFriend(String) rather than case duplicateFriend.
Use guard for error conditions and if let for the ordinary unwrap.
Use typed throws (throws(MyError)) only for internal functions, error-forwarding generic code and constrained environments; use untyped throws for public API.
Force-unwrap only where you can state the invariant, and prefer a failing #require or precondition with a message over a bare !.
Start every app entirely on the main thread.

Add concurrency in this order without skipping steps: single-threaded on the main actor; async/await to hide latency; @concurrent for your expensive work only after Instruments shows a hang; actor only when too much main-actor state forces tasks to hop back constantly.
Enable the Approachable Concurrency build setting in every project.
For app and UI-facing modules set Default Actor Isolation to MainActor; in a package use swiftSettings: [.defaultIsolation(MainActor.self)].
Do not set main-actor-by-default for a general-purpose library; ship nonisolated APIs and let clients decide where work runs.
Do not rely on async to move work off the current actor; mark your own CPU-heavy functions @concurrent to switch to the concurrent thread pool.
Use nonisolated as the default isolation for library APIs, not @MainActor or @concurrent; nonisolated on a type makes all its members nonisolated (Swift 6.1+).
Profile with Instruments (Time Profiler, hangs) before offloading work, and make code faster without concurrency first whenever possible.
Do not spawn a task for trivial work such as reading a UserDefaults value.
Use one task per end-to-end operation: put work that must happen in order in one task and give independent operations separate tasks.
Re-check assumptions after every await, never hold a lock across an await, and never rely on thread-local storage across one.
Mutate actor state in synchronous methods.
Keep async actor methods thin, composed of synchronous transactional operations, and leave the actor consistent at every await.
After awaiting a download inside an actor, re-check the cache before writing it, or dedupe the in-flight work.
Do not use an actor to guarantee ordering; use a task or an AsyncStream.
Use an actor or a @MainActor class for shared mutable state, not a class plus a lock you must remember.
Move work off the main thread with a @concurrent async function, not Task.detached or DispatchQueue.global().
Never use a blocking primitive such as DispatchSemaphore or NSCondition across an await; restructure instead.
Write Sendable explicitly on public types that should be shareable.

Keep most model classes neither @MainActor nor Sendable (a shared model class is non-Sendable or @MainActor, never Sendable plus manual locking); if one must leave the main actor, make it nonisolated rather than Sendable.
When sending a non-Sendable object to another isolation domain, make all mutations before the hand-off and do not touch it afterwards.
Mark a function type @Sendable only if it genuinely crosses isolation domains.
Reserve @unchecked Sendable for types with real internal synchronization (a Mutex or a lock), and use nonisolated(unsafe) on a global only as a last resort, never to silence a warning.

Fix a data-race error in this order: stop sharing (move the object into a local per job); make it a Sendable value type; isolate it to an actor; only then use Mutex/Atomic from the Synchronization module (in let properties) or @unchecked Sendable.
Fix global and static variables in this order of preference: make it a let; put it on @MainActor; wrap it in a Mutex; nonisolated(unsafe).

Bridge old callback APIs by annotating delegate protocols you own with @MainActor; for ones you do not own, mark the method nonisolated and use MainActor.assumeIsolated { } (or @preconcurrency on the conformance).
Prefer structured tasks (async let, task groups) over unstructured ones.
Use async let for a fixed, statically known number of concurrent children, not N unstructured Tasks.
Use withTaskGroup when the number of children is dynamic, iterating results as they land.
Use withDiscardingTaskGroup when children return nothing, not a withTaskGroup you never drain.

Use Task { } only when the work's lifetime does not fit a scope (a delegate callback, a button tap, a view appearing): open it inside the synchronous callback rather than making the callback async, and manage its cancellation yourself.
Almost never use Task.detached; if you need a detached root, put a task group inside it rather than detaching repeatedly.
Check Task.isCancelled or try Task.checkCancellation() before starting expensive work, in synchronous helpers too.
For suspended work such as an AsyncSequence's next(), use withTaskCancellationHandler and protect the state it touches with an atomic or a lock, not an actor.
Bound concurrency: start N children, then add a new one each time one finishes, instead of one child per item over an unbounded list.
Propagate context such as a request ID or trace span with @TaskLocal values, and make them optional.
When bridging callbacks with withCheckedContinuation or withCheckedThrowingContinuation, resume exactly once on every path; for delegate APIs, store the continuation and nil it out when you resume.

Iterate async sequences with for await / for try await, and adapt handler- or delegate-based APIs with AsyncStream / AsyncThrowingStream: construct the source inside the closure, yield from the handler, clean up in onTermination.
Do not add @MainActor to SwiftUI views or view models (you almost never need it); with main-actor-by-default, delete the ones you have.
Inside SwiftUI closures marked @Sendable (visualEffect, Shape.path(in:), Layout requirements, onGeometryChange), copy the one value you need into the capture list instead of capturing self.

Start animations for gestures and scroll events with a withAnimation state change inside SwiftUI's synchronous action callback, on the same frame as the event, and open a Task only for the long-running work that follows; do not make the callback async.
Put a piece of state on the seam between UI and async work: the view starts a task, the async layer does a synchronous mutation when it finishes, and the UI reacts.
